session.question: What clinical and laboratory findings are associated with elevated FSH in men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, and how do KS and testicular XX DSD compare with the undefined cause group?
session.answer:
Elevated serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are indicative of testicular dysfunction in men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) related to chromosomal anomalies. Specifically, patients with Klinefelter syndrome (KS) exhibit significantly higher serum FSH levels compared to men with undefined causes of NOA. In addition to elevated FSH, the KS group presents with distinct clinical features such as lower mean testicular volume, shorter penile length, decreased total testosterone levels, and a higher incidence of gynecomastia (unknownauthorsUnknownyearclinicalandlaboratory chunk 1).

Conversely, individuals with testicular XX disorder of sexual development (DSD) show FSH and LH levels that are intermediate between those found in KS patients and the undefined cause group. While the testicular volume for the testicular XX DSD group is comparable to that of the KS patients, the penile length measurements fall between KS and the undefined causes. Other clinical characteristics align closer with those in the undefined group, indicating a broader spectrum of hormonal responses among these chromosomal anomalies (unknownauthorsUnknownyearclinicalandlaboratory chunk 1). 

These findings emphasize the importance of distinguishing between chromosomal diagnoses to guide clinical management effectively.
